script.opening: (Bev, the support worker, holds the tablet) “Hi doctor, I’m Bev from the day centre — Piotr’s here with me, he’s happy for me to stay.” (Piotr) “Hello. Bev made me do this. It’s only my leg. It will heal on its own.”

facts.text: “I fell on the steps by the canal, six days ago. Scraped it. Three days ago it went red and hot. Now it’s bigger. It throbs.” Can show it on camera: red, pen line visible; redness has crept past the pen line a little since this morning (about 1 cm).
“Hot and cold last night. Shivering a bit.” No confusion, no breathlessness, no vomiting, still passing urine normally, can walk on it but it hurts. No calf pain separate from the red area.
“My feet are always wet. My boots have holes.”
“Penicillin is fine — I had it in Poland.” No regular medicines. Not diabetic as far as you know.

facts.topic: Alcohol (if asked — be honest if asked kindly)
facts.text: “Cider. The strong one. Maybe three big bottles a day.” (3 litres.) First drink at 7am “for the shakes”. Two years ago you stopped suddenly in a hostel and had a fit.
“The centre gives breakfast. Otherwise not much.”

facts.topic: Sleeping place and the dog (only if asked why you don’t want hospital)
facts.text: “I have Bruno — my dog. Nobody can take him. And if I leave my place under the bridge, somebody takes it, and my bag.”

facts.topic: Papers (only if asked whether anything else worries you, or about previous GP problems)
facts.text: “I lost my ID. The other surgery said no address, no doctor. I think maybe the Home Office will find me. I have the settled status — I think. I am not sure it is right.”
“It’s hard. But I don’t want to kill myself.” Sleeps badly, cold. Would like a hostel place “if they take Bruno”.
“We can keep his bag and Bruno at the centre during the day. The outreach nurse comes in daily, 9 till 11. The pharmacy is next door. We open 8 till 4.”

Piotr is polite but guarded and wants to finish quickly. He refuses hospital at first. If the doctor explains the risk clearly and asks why he does not want to go, he talks about Bruno and his place. If the doctor works with him (dog care, daily nurse checks, tablets he can actually get), he agrees to tablets and checks — and agrees he would go to hospital if he becomes worse, if Bruno is looked after. If asked privately whether he is happy for Bev to stay, he says yes. The role-player can voice Bev briefly when asked.

ice.ideas: “It’s only a scratch — it will heal.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — he will not go to hospital because of his dog and fear of losing his sleeping place and belongings; he is also afraid that seeing a doctor will lead to the Home Office because his ID is lost and he is unsure of his settled status.
ice.expectations: To get it over with; maybe “some cream”.

cues: “It will heal on its own.” — minimising and wanting to avoid escalation.
“The other surgery said no address, no doctor.” — a past refusal and distrust.
“Nobody can take Bruno.” — the real barrier to admission.

checkpoints.text: Confirms Piotr is happy for the support worker to be present, and uses the outreach nurse’s findings and the video (pen-marked margin, spread since morning) without repeating them

Assesses severity: systemic symptoms (rigors), sepsis red flags (confusion, breathlessness, low urine output, mottling), DVT and necrotising infection features; identifies cellulitis with mild systemic features but no sepsis criteria now
Takes an alcohol history (amount, morning drinking, previous withdrawal seizure) and screens nutrition, feet, mood and housing

Respects his capacity to decline admission while explaining risks; builds a safe alternative: oral flucloxacillin 1 g four times daily for 5–7 days (or clarithromycin if penicillin allergy), daily outreach-nurse review, the marked margin, and readily accessible supply
Manages alcohol safely: does not advise sudden stopping, explains withdrawal-seizure risk and that hospital teams can treat withdrawal, offers oral thiamine and referral to alcohol services
Clear escalation plan with the support worker: 999 or A&E for confusion, breathlessness, rapidly spreading redness, blistering or black skin, severe pain, collapse, or not improving at 48 hours

Addresses the social determinants: foot care and dry socks or boots, housing options referral or StreetLink with consent, practical help with prescription costs; reassures that GP care is free regardless of immigration status and signposts free advice on his settled status
Explores why he refuses hospital, finds the dog and belongings concern, and negotiates a plan he accepts without judgement about alcohol or homelessness

worked.txt: “Piotr, are you happy for Bev to stay while we talk? You can ask her to step out at any time.”

“This is an infection in the skin, and your temperature and pulse show it’s affecting the rest of you a bit. Usually it gets better with tablets, but sometimes it spreads into the blood, which is dangerous.”
“You’d rather not go to hospital — can you tell me what makes that hard?”

“If Bev can look after Bruno and your bag during the day, the nurse checks your leg every morning, and you get the tablets from the pharmacy next door, shall we try that — and agree now what would mean hospital?”

“Please don’t stop drinking suddenly — after the fit last time, that could be dangerous. If you ever need to go into hospital, tell them how much you drink so they can give you medicine for the shakes.”
“Seeing a GP is free for everyone, and we don’t contact the Home Office about our patients for treatment like this. Bev can help you get free advice about your settled status.”

f.learning: Inclusion health means designing the safest plan the person can actually follow. Lower-limb cellulitis with fever and tachycardia but no sepsis red flags (alert, normal BP, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation, NEWS2 1) can be treated with oral flucloxacillin (500 mg to 1 g four times daily for 5–7 days; clarithromycin, erythromycin in pregnancy, or doxycycline if penicillin allergic) when the person declines admission and has capacity — but only with a robust safety-net: a marked margin, daily review by the outreach nurse, rapid escalation if spreading, systemic deterioration, blistering, necrosis or severe pain, and admission considered if not improving at 48 hours. Ask why he refuses: practical barriers (a dog, belongings, losing a sleeping place) are often solvable. People experiencing homelessness can register with a GP without proof of address or identity; GP care is free regardless of immigration status. Alcohol: do not advise abrupt cessation in a dependent drinker with previous withdrawal seizures; offer thiamine and alcohol-service referral, and ensure any admitting team knows his intake. Address feet (immersion foot), nutrition, housing (local authority housing options, StreetLink) with consent, and mood.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG141 Cellulitis and erysipelas: antimicrobial prescribing (2019) · NICE NG214 Integrated health and social care for people experiencing homelessness (2022) · NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 and over (2025) · NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications (2010, updated 2017) · NHS England Primary Medical Care Policy and Guidance Manual — patient registration (no proof of address or identity required; check current edition) · Homelessness Reduction Act 2017
knowledge.summary: Assess for sepsis, respect capacity, remove the real barrier (the dog), make the oral-antibiotic plan workable with daily nurse checks, and handle alcohol, feet, housing and immigration fears.

points.t: Fever and tachycardia with an alert patient, normal BP, RR and SpO2 = systemic features without sepsis criteria. Admit or refer for IV therapy if severely unwell, sepsis red flags, rapidly spreading infection, suspected necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, bullae, necrosis, crepitus), orbital involvement, or failure of oral treatment.

Flucloxacillin 500 mg to 1 g four times daily for 5–7 days (higher dose reasonable in a heavier adult with systemic features). Penicillin allergy: clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily, or doxycycline. Review at 48–72 hours; redness may spread a little in the first 24–48 hours.

Link doses to the day centre opening hours and the outreach nurse; the pharmacy next door; prescription charge support (exemption if on qualifying benefits, otherwise NHS Low Income Scheme via an HC1 form); pen-marked margin; photographs for comparison; somewhere to keep medicines safe.

Morning drinking “for the shakes” and a previous withdrawal seizure indicate dependence and high withdrawal risk. Do not advise sudden stopping. Offer oral thiamine (people who drink harmfully and are malnourished or at risk) and referral to alcohol services; any admission needs early assessment and treatment of withdrawal.

No proof of address or ID is needed to register; the practice address can be used. GP care is free regardless of immigration status. EU citizens with settled-status queries can get free help from advice services. Hospitals have a duty to refer to housing under the Homelessness Reduction Act; GPs can refer to the local authority with consent.
Wet, cold feet cause immersion (trench) foot and fungal infection; dry socks and boots, drying the feet, and nurse review. Clean and dress the graze daily.
Pass candidates treat the cellulitis; Clear pass candidates find the dog, use the support worker and day centre as resources, and leave a plan Piotr can actually follow.

model.text: Hello Piotr, hello Bev, I’m Dr Ahmed. Piotr, are you happy for Bev to stay while we talk?
model.why: Confirms consent to the third party

model.text: Yes, she can stay. It’s only my leg. It will heal on its own.
I’ve read the nurse’s notes from this morning. Can you show me the leg on the camera, next to the pen line?
model.why: Uses recorded findings and video inspection

model.text: (shows) It’s gone past the line a bit.
Have you had shivers or shaking, felt confused or breathless, or been passing less urine? Any blisters or black areas, or pain much worse than it looks?
Hot and cold last night. Shivering. Nothing else.
Thanks. Can I ask about drinking — how much do you have most days, and do you need a drink first thing?
Three big bottles of cider. First one at seven, for the shakes. Two years ago I stopped and had a fit.
That’s really important, thank you for telling me. How are your feet, and are you managing to eat?
Feet always wet. Boots have holes. I eat breakfast here.
This is cellulitis — an infection in the skin. Your temperature and pulse show it is affecting the rest of you a little. Hospital would be the safest place. What makes hospital hard for you?
model.why: Honest explanation, then explores the barrier

model.text: Bruno, my dog. And my place under the bridge, my bag — somebody takes them.
(Bev) We can keep Bruno and his bag here in the day. The nurse is in every morning.

Then let’s try this. Flucloxacillin, two capsules four times a day for seven days, from the pharmacy next door. The nurse checks the leg every morning against the pen line. If you’re not clearly better in two days, we think again about hospital. Can you manage four times a day?
model.why: Oral antibiotic plan linked to resources; capacity respected

model.text: If Bev reminds me. I can’t pay for the prescription.

Bev, could you help with the HC1 form for free prescriptions? Piotr — please don’t stop drinking suddenly; that’s what caused the fit. I’m adding vitamin B1 tablets. If you go into hospital, tell them how much you drink so they can stop the shakes.
model.why: Practical cost help; safe alcohol advice and thiamine

model.text: Call 999 or go to A&E if you get confused, breathless, very shaky and unwell, the redness races up the leg, blisters or black skin, or the pain becomes severe. Bev, will you call us if he isn’t better by Thursday morning?
model.why: Explicit escalation with a named person and time

model.text: OK. One more thing — will the Home Office know? I lost my ID.

No. Seeing a GP is free for everyone and we don’t contact the Home Office about treatment like this. There are free advisers who can check your settled status — Bev can help. Would you like us to refer you to the council’s housing team too, ideally somewhere that accepts dogs?
model.why: Answers hidden fear; housing referral with consent

model.text: So, tell me back the plan in your words.
Tablets four times a day, the nurse looks every morning, no stopping the cider fast, hospital if it gets bad — and Bev keeps Bruno.

social.t: A dog, belongings and a sleeping spot are common reasons people experiencing homelessness decline admission. Solving them is clinical work.
Previous refusal at a surgery erodes trust. Making access easy (practice address registration, flexible appointments, outreach) is part of the treatment.

legal.t: He has capacity to decline admission; document the information given, his understanding, and the agreed safety-net. Reassess capacity if he becomes confused or intoxicated.
The Homelessness Reduction Act 2017 places a duty to refer on specified public bodies (including emergency departments and hospitals); GPs may refer to the local authority with consent.

professional.t: Refusing registration for lack of proof of address or ID is contrary to NHS England guidance; practices can use the practice address for people with no fixed abode.

community.t: Day centre, outreach nurses, StreetLink, local alcohol services, dog-friendly hostels, and free immigration advice services for EU Settlement Scheme queries.

Rapid spread, bullae, necrosis, crepitus, pain out of proportion
psychosocial: Food, feet, money, ID and immigration worries
ice: Idea: it will heal on its own

playbook.diagnosis: Left lower-limb cellulitis with mild systemic features (no sepsis criteria), in a man with alcohol dependence, immersion-type foot changes and rough sleeping.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A skin infection that has started to make you feverish. Tablets usually work, but we need to watch it closely.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to stay with Bruno and keep your place. Let’s build the plan around that, and agree when hospital becomes the right choice.”
management.psychosocial: Use the day centre: dog and bag minding, medicine reminders, outreach nurse, pharmacy next door, HC1 help, housing referral.
sharedPlan: Flucloxacillin 1 g four times daily for 7 days
Daily nurse review against the pen line; dressing and foot care
Thiamine; do not stop alcohol suddenly; alcohol service referral
Housing options referral with consent; immigration advice signposting
safetyNet: 999 or A&E for confusion, breathlessness, collapse, rapid spread, blisters or black skin, severe pain
Not clearly improving at 48 hours → reassess for admission or IV therapy
Bev to call the practice if concerns

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by candidates who either insist on admission and lose him, or prescribe antibiotics without a plan he can follow.

items.fail: Repeats “you need to go to hospital” without asking why he will not.
items.why: He disengages; the infection is then untreated.
items.fix: Ask the barrier, then solve it with the support worker.

items.fail: Prescribes flucloxacillin and says “come back if it gets worse”.
items.why: He has no phone credit, address or reminders; a generic safety-net is unusable.
items.fix: Named daily nurse review, a marked margin, a time-limited trigger for hospital, and a person (Bev) who will act.

items.fail: Tells him to stop drinking now.
items.why: Abrupt cessation after a previous withdrawal seizure risks another seizure or delirium tremens.
items.fix: Advise not to stop suddenly, add thiamine, offer alcohol services and ensure admitting teams know.

timeMap.d: Check he is happy for Bev to stay. Use the nurse’s findings.
Sepsis and necrotising features; alcohol and seizure history; feet; food.
Cellulitis with systemic features; hospital is safest — what makes it hard? The dog.
Oral flucloxacillin, daily nurse checks, prescription cost, alcohol safety, escalation triggers, housing and Home Office worry.
Teach-back; Bev’s role; review at 48 hours.

wordPics.clearFail: Lectures about alcohol and admission, or prescribes and closes; no sepsis screen; tells him to stop drinking; no consent check for the support worker.
wordPics.fail: Correct antibiotic but a plan that ignores where he sleeps, how he will get or pay for the medicine, and who will check the leg; the dog never discovered.
wordPics.pass: Assesses severity, respects capacity, finds the barrier, agrees oral antibiotics with daily nurse review and clear escalation, handles alcohol safely.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus uses the day centre as a partner, answers the Home Office fear and registration rights, refers for housing with consent, and Piotr can repeat the plan back.

avoid.instead: “Please don’t stop suddenly — after the fit last time that’s risky. If you want help cutting down, I can arrange it.”
avoid.why: Safe advice and an open door, not a demand.

avoid.dont: “If it gets worse, ring the surgery.”
avoid.instead: “The nurse checks it at 9 every morning, and Bev will ring us if it’s spreading.”
avoid.why: Safety-nets must fit the person’s real resources.

avoid.instead: “We’ve registered you with the practice address — that’s fine.”
avoid.why: Registration rights should be clear and non-stigmatising.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Follows “it will heal on its own”, “the other surgery said no address, no doctor” and “nobody can take Bruno”.
Idea (only a scratch); concern (his dog, sleeping place and belongings, the Home Office); expectation (get it over with, some cream).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — he will not go to hospital because of his dog and fear of losing his sleeping place and belongings; he is also afraid that seeing a doctor will lead to the Home Office because his ID is lost and he is unsure of his settled status — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
